chunks: Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdullah, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'The Takbeer during the days of Tashreeq is at the end of the prayers.' He said: 'The Takbeer in Mina is at the end of fifteen prayers; and in the other cities, it is at the end of ten prayers.'

And the first Takbeer is at the end of the Dhuhr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), saying in it: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illa Allahu wa Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd. Allahu Akbar 'ala ma hadana, Allahu Akbar 'ala ma razaqana min bahimat al-an'am.'

And it was made to be in the other cities at the end of ten prayers because when the people leave in the first departure, the people of the cities withhold from the Takbeer, and the people of Mina continue to Takbeer as long as they are in Mina until the final departure.

key_terms.دُبُرِ الصَّلَوَاتِ: At the end of the prayers
key_terms.يَوْمَ النَّحْرِ: The Day of Sacrifice (10th Dhu al-Hijjah)

ai.seo_question: What is the correct number of prayers after which Takbeer is recited during the Days of Tashreeq in Mina versus other cities?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the distinct jurisprudential rulings for the public recitation of Takbeer al-Tashreeq, differentiating between the extended duration in Mina (fifteen prayers) and the abbreviated period in other cities (ten prayers) to account for the timing of the pilgrims' departure. It highlights the scholarly emphasis on communal worship and the specific liturgical formula, which echoes the Quranic themes of gratitude for divine provision and the ritual of sacrifice.
